name: Dark Violet-Grey
lede: Dark Violet-Grey is a near-neutral, barely purple grey recorded by Ridgway in 1912 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a dark bluish gray, despite its violet name.

sections.title: A violet almost without color
sections.body:
The name traces to violet, a plant-and-landscape word in our data, but by the time it reaches this dark a grey, almost none of that color remains [1]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas plots it on plate LII at hue 59′′′′′, tone k [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same area as block 234, calling it a "dark bluish gray" rather than a violet, about 0.9 units from that block's reference point[1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 35, chroma 4, hue 241 degrees: dark and almost without saturation [1].

Its parent family word is [[dark-violet]], the fuller-colored version this grey mutes down [1]. Its nearest distinct neighbors by computed color distance are [[dark-violet-slate|Dark Violet-Slate]] and [[dark-blue-slate|Dark Blue-Slate]], both 3.1 units away and read in our data as "almost the same" [2]. A third close neighbor is [[blackish-plumbeous|Blackish Plumbeous]], 3.6 units off, also "almost the same" [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 225, as photographed, more common than 72 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 2.4 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive [3]. Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec is its most devoted painter here, with the color present in 4 of 36 of his works in the archive, well above the baseline of the museums those works come from [3].
